title: The Playbook We've Already Used Three Times — Eddie Would Go

The Playbook We've Already Used Three Times
July 2026 · Geopolitics · Technology · United States · China
"Those who are skilled in war bring the enemy to the battlefield and are not brought there by him."
— Sun Tzu, The Art of War, ch. VI

There is a pattern China has already executed three times, with three almost identical results. In solar panels, it invested more than 50 billion dollars in state subsidies, sold below cost until non-Chinese manufacturers collapsed, and today controls most of world manufacturing. In rare earths, it went from controlling 21% of global supply in 1985 to 97% in 2010 —and today processes close to 70% of the twenty strategic minerals the International Energy Agency considers critical. In lithium batteries and electric vehicles, the same script: more than 230 billion dollars in subsidies accumulated since 2009, prices below real cost, and a dominant position that today lets it set the pace of the entire supply chain de facto.
The question this piece poses is simple: is the same thing happening, right now, with artificial intelligence?
I. The same book, read differently

The empirical evidence suggests it is. DeepSeek V4 Flash costs 0.28 dollars per million output tokens. GPT-5.5, OpenAI's flagship model, costs 30 dollars for the same unit —more than a hundred times more. Alibaba's Qwen, Zhipu AI's GLM, and MiniMax complete a range of open-source Chinese models running between 60% and 90% cheaper than their American equivalents, according to Justin Summerville, of OpenRouter.

THE DATA — Cost per million output tokens: the five most used Chinese models cost between $0.28 and $4.40. The five benchmark American models cost between $5 and $180. See the full table at the end of the text.

The result, measured in real traffic rather than promises: models of Chinese origin have sustained a share of at least 30% of enterprise token volume every week since 8 February 2026, with a weekly peak of 46%. Twelve months earlier, that number averaged barely 11%. In the first half of 2025, it was 4.5%. The week of 9 to 15 February 2026 marked the crossover: for the first time, the volume of tokens processed by Chinese models exceeded that of American ones in absolute terms.

This is not a technical curiosity. It is the same curve Chinese solar panels traced between 2008 and 2013, before Washington and Brussels reacted with anti-dumping tariffs when it was already too late to save most Western manufacturers.
II. American companies, running towards the discount

The list of American companies already running Chinese models in production is no longer marginal. Airbnb confirmed, through its own CEO Brian Chesky, that it runs Alibaba's Qwen for customer service, describing it as “fast and cheap”. Coinbase, according to statements by its CEO Brian Armstrong on X, runs GLM-5.2 and Kimi in production and cut its AI spending almost in half even as its token consumption rose. Shopify, Perplexity, Nvidia and Siemens have been publicly linked to the use of Qwen. Cursor (Anysphere) uses Kimi, from Moonshot AI. Microsoft is evaluating a fine-tuned version of DeepSeek V4 as a low-cost engine for Copilot Cowork.

Two committees of the United States House of Representatives opened a formal investigation into Airbnb and Anysphere over the use of these models, citing risks of data security, censorship and a possible systematic campaign of distillation of Western models by Chinese laboratories —an accusation Anthropic and OpenAI had already formalised before Congress in February 2026.

The technical sector itself supplies a second layer of evidence, less ideological and more uncomfortable: a Booz Allen Hamilton study from May 2026, with more than 2,800 tests across five code-generation models —four Chinese and one American— found that three of the four Chinese models produced significantly more vulnerabilities when the prompt suggested a United States government user, with Qwen3-Coder generating 130% more. The four Chinese models also systematically refused tasks Beijing considers sensitive. It is not only a price war: it is a price war with a layer of structural risk that the companies migrating are, in most cases, ignoring.
III. The other half of the equation: an economy staked on a single number

This is where the argument becomes more uncomfortable for Washington than for Beijing. According to Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo Global Management, economic activity linked to artificial intelligence accounts for roughly half of all United States GDP growth in 2026. Other calculations, based on Bureau of Economic Analysis data and on companies' quarterly results, are more extreme still: capital spending on AI infrastructure represented close to 75% of all American GDP growth in the first quarter of 2026. Without that spending, the economy would have been, in practice, stagnant.

THE DATA — Concentration of the economy in AI: Google, Amazon, Microsoft and Meta together plan some USD 725 billion of capital spending in 2026. Half of all corporate debt issued this year is linked to AI —15% of the entire corporate bond market. Technology and adjacent companies represent 50% of the total value of the S&P 500.

The capital spending to cash flow ratio of the large hyperscalers —Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta— is approaching 75%, a level that analysts such as Ed Yardeni, the economist who coined the term “bond vigilantes”, compare directly to the excesses of 1999. The difference, the optimists say, is that today's companies have real earnings behind the spending. The question nobody can answer yet is whether those earnings survive a market where the price of the principal input —the token— is collapsing 90% because of Chinese competition.
IV. Where the two theses meet

On 20 July 2026 —today— Nvidia is trading approximately 14% below its 2026 high, and the Philadelphia semiconductor index has entered a technical bear market. The reason financial analysts themselves cite is not a fall in demand for compute: it is the doubt over whether the hyperscalers can keep converting capital spending into revenue, just as open-source Chinese models threaten to compress the inference market —the segment Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, called the dominant AI workload of 2026.

A technology investor put it without nuance on X, in a post echoed by several financial outlets in June: if companies migrate their AI spending from millions of dollars to a fraction of that, the valuations of OpenAI and Anthropic —and with them much of the scaffolding of debt and capital that holds the sector up— could collapse. “The bubble is not AI. It is the price of AI. And it is about to burst”, he wrote. Firms such as Futurum Group came out to qualify that forecast, but nobody serious in the market now denies the underlying premise.
V. The week that sums up the whole argument

If a single week were needed to see the two theses of this piece collide in real time, it was this one. On 16 July, Moonshot AI —the Chinese laboratory behind the Kimi assistant— launched Kimi K3: 2.8 trillion parameters, the largest open-source model ever published, with a context window of one million tokens. According to independent evaluations by Artificial Analysis and Vals AI, K3 beats Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 on several coding benchmarks and long-horizon agentic tasks, at a fraction of the price —15 dollars per million output tokens, against 25 for Opus and 30 for GPT-5.5. The launch triggered an immediate fall in semiconductor stocks on the Nasdaq and Tokyo's Nikkei, before most analysts had even finished reading the technical documentation.

The timing was not accidental. The following day, 17 July, Xi Jinping gave the opening address of the World AI Conference (WAIC) in Shanghai and announced the creation of the World AI Cooperation Organisation (WAICO), headquartered in Shanghai, along with 5,000 new AI training scholarships for developing countries over five years. Xi called for the development of AI “not to be a solo show by a single country, but a symphony of international cooperation”, and criticised what he called the “overstretching” of national security concerns by other countries —a barely veiled reference to the American export controls that already once suspended Anthropic's most advanced models.
"The development of AI should not be a solo show by a single country, but a symphony of international cooperation."
— Xi Jinping, opening address of the World AI Conference, Shanghai, 17 July 2026

The South China Morning Post itself noted the parallel: Xi's speech came only hours after Trump, in a prime-time national broadcast, accused China of orchestrating “the largest compromise of electoral data in history”. Two speeches on the same day, in opposite directions: one offering open cooperation and free models to the Global South, the other denouncing a threat to democratic integrity. The contrast could not better illustrate the central thesis of this piece —while Washington debates the framing of the threat, Beijing is already giving away the infrastructure.
VI. What we still do not know

Neither the parallel with solar dumping nor the parallel with the bubble of 1999 is, as yet, an accomplished fact. The difference with solar is that there was no actor on the Western side with the capital and scale of today's American hyperscalers: Google, Microsoft, Amazon and Meta can absorb years of spending that no European or American solar manufacturer could. And the difference with 1999 is that, unlike the dot-coms, the companies leading the spending today have real operating profits, not just promises.

But the pattern of Chinese behaviour —state subsidy, deliberate overcapacity, prices no free-market competitor can match, followed by a dominant position that then allows it to set the terms— is, according to evidence gathered by FDD, the IEA and the United States Congress itself, a pattern that has repeated with a consistency that no longer admits the word “coincidence”. The question left open is not whether China is competing. It is whether, as with solar and rare earths, by the time Washington reacts seriously it will already be too late for the reaction to change the outcome.
